clinicalPearls: A rare multisystem disorder caused by gain-of-function variants in the L-type calcium channel gene CACNA1C, classified as long QT syndrome type 8
Marked QT prolongation predisposes to life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death, often in infancy or early childhood
Extracardiac features commonly include cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers and toes, facial dysmorphism, and neurodevelopmental problems such as autism spectrum features
Congenital heart defects, immune dysfunction, hypoglycaemia and dental abnormalities can also occur
The classic form usually arises from de novo variants, so a negative family history does not exclude it
Management focuses on preventing arrhythmia with beta-blockers, careful avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs and an implantable cardioverter defibrillator in high-risk children
Functional 2:1 atrioventricular block can occur because the very long ventricular repolarisation leaves the ventricle refractory to alternate atrial beats
Care is multidisciplinary given the cardiac, developmental and systemic involvement
reference.pathophysiology: Timothy syndrome is caused by gain-of-function variants in CACNA1C, which encodes the pore-forming subunit of the L-type calcium channel (CaV1.2). The variants impair voltage-dependent inactivation of the channel, so calcium entry into cells is prolonged. In cardiomyocytes this lengthens the action potential and markedly prolongs the QT interval, promoting early afterdepolarisations and torsades-de-pointes ventricular arrhythmia. Because CaV1.2 is expressed widely, the same channel dysfunction disrupts development and function of other tissues, producing the syndactyly, neurodevelopmental, immune and other systemic features that distinguish the syndrome from isolated long QT syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Other genetic long QT syndrome subtypes
Acquired QT prolongation from drugs or electrolyte disturbance
Other syndromic causes of syndactyly with cardiac disease
Congenital heart block from other causes
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG demonstrating marked QT prolongation and any functional 2:1 atrioventricular block
Echocardiography for associated congenital heart defects
Evaluation of immune function, glucose homeostasis and dental health as indicated
redFlags: Marked QT prolongation with syncope or documented ventricular arrhythmia
Functional 2:1 atrioventricular block in an infant
Syndactyly with cardiac and neurodevelopmental features prompting urgent cardiac evaluation
reference.prognosis: Timothy syndrome carries a high risk of early sudden death from malignant ventricular arrhythmia, and survivors face substantial neurodevelopmental and systemic morbidity; multidisciplinary care and arrhythmia prevention improve but do not eliminate the risk.
pitfalls: Assuming a negative family history excludes the diagnosis, when most cases are de novo
Attributing an infant's QT prolongation to reversible causes and missing the genetic syndrome
Focusing on the cardiac problem and overlooking the syndactyly and developmental clues
Using QT-prolonging medications that can precipitate torsades
Underestimating the systemic and immune complications
references: ESC Guidelines for the management of patients with ventricular arrhythmias and the prevention of sudden cardiac death
management: Prevent arrhythmia with beta-blockade as the cornerstone of cardiac management
Strictly avoid QT-prolonging drugs and correct electrolyte disturbances that further lengthen the QT interval
Implant a cardioverter defibrillator in high-risk children, and consider left cardiac sympathetic denervation for breakthrough arrhythmia
Treat acute torsades-de-pointes with magnesium and defibrillation, with a calcium channel blocker such as verapamil considered given the underlying L-type calcium channel gain of function
Provide multidisciplinary support for extracardiac features, including surgical release of syndactyly, neurodevelopmental and autism support, and attention to immune, glucose and dental problems
Monitor with serial ECG, QT assessment and ambulatory rhythm recording, and screen for congenital heart defects with echocardiography
Offer genetic counselling and cardiac evaluation of relatives, recognising that most cases arise from de novo variants so a negative family history does not exclude it
